Resolve the block-kosh parimana 96 vs 64 question (32 bytes, diagnostic only): koshes created INSIDE a mandapa cost 96 (not 64 outside) and persist at 96 after the block (BlockB: 0->96->96). Whether 96 is right (real block-kosh tracking memory that persists because the kosh persists) or a 32-byte overcount/leak per block-kosh (tracking that should be freed after the block decides the kosh persists, but is not) cannot be determined from parimana() alone (both give 96 after block). Not a program-correctness defect (programs work correctly, values correct, no crash/silent wrong - only the reported number differs by 32 bytes per block-kosh) and not a sign-off blocker, but worth one line in release notes or a follow-up probe (e.g., grow a block kosh after the block and see if the 32 bytes are needed for growth, or if they are dead).

param_growth_message.full_message: Only one line, no error code, no hint: 'Sutram truti: kosh-tarke kosh_push asamarthitam' (kosh_push unsupported for kosh parameters).
param_growth_message.is_it_right: NO, it is NOT the right message, for three reasons: (1) Wrong name: says kosh_push (old, deprecated name), but the program used kosh_kship (current name, since v292) - a user who wrote kosh_kship gets an error saying kosh_push is unsupported, confusing (they did not write kosh_push). (2) No error code: unlike E_KOSH_DVARA/E_VITTI_PRAKAR (which have codes), this refusal has no E_* code - inconsistent, harder to reference in docs or bug reports. (3) No hint: unlike other refusals (which have a Sanket: line telling the user what to do instead), this one gives no guidance (e.g., 'grow the kosh in the caller, then pass it; or return the grown kosh from the function'). The REFUSAL itself (parameter growth unsupported) is correct and safe (as established in R129 - parameters are shared for reading (bounds-checked), but growth via parameters would update a copy, not the caller's descriptor, so v303 refuses rather than allowing a stale caller descriptor). Only the MESSAGE is wrong. Diagnostic nit, not a crash/silent wrong, and not a sign-off blocker for a release candidate (see WS2) - but should be fixed before final release (trivial: change kosh_push -> kosh_kship, add an E_* code, add a hint).

parimana.after_20k: Program: parimana() before and after creating 20,000 koshes (each 1 element, 4-cap, via make_kosh()), then last[0]. Result: 0, 1280000, 19999. 1,280,000 = 20,000 x 64 (exactly, descriptor + buffer per kosh, 16-aligned). Not 0, not 1.28 TB (old regions), not overcounted. RIGHT.
parimana.after_block: Clean tests (no prior koshes, to isolate): Block with nirmmita only (16 bytes scratch): 0 -> 16 (inside) -> 0 (after) - RIGHT (scratch freed, no block overhead leak, back to 0). Block with kosh only (1 element, 4-cap): 0 -> 96 (inside) -> 96 (after) - kosh persists (right, koshes outlive blocks), but costs 96, not 64 (outside-block kosh cost). Kosh outside block first, then block with nirmmita only: 64 (kosh) -> 80 (inside: 64+16, correct) -> 64 (after: back to 64, nirmmita freed, kosh persists, no leak) - RIGHT. Original block test (nirmmita + kosh in block, then kosh outside): 0 -> 16 -> 112 -> 96 -> 192 - consistent with clean tests (block kosh 96, persists at 96 after block (only nirmmita 16 freed), then new outside kosh adds 96 (not 64) in this sequence - same block-kosh anomaly (see open question), not a separate issue. OPEN QUESTION (minor, diagnostic only, not program correctness): koshes created INSIDE a mandapa (and, in the sequence above, the next kosh after a block) cost 96, not 64 (outside-block kosh cost). Whether 96 is RIGHT (real block-kosh tracking memory, e.g., 32 bytes for block-kosh bookkeeping that persists because the kosh persists) or a 32-byte overcount/leak per block-kosh (tracking that should be freed after the block decides the kosh persists, but is not) cannot be determined from parimana() alone (both give 96 after block). NOT a program-correctness defect (programs work correctly, values correct, no crash/silent wrong - only the reported number differs by 32 bytes per block-kosh) and NOT a sign-off blocker (see WS2), but worth one line in release notes or a follow-up probe (e.g., grow a block kosh after the block and see if the 32 bytes are needed for growth, or if they are dead).
parimana.after_growth: Program: parimana() at 5 points (start; after 1-element 4-cap kosh; after 4 elements (no growth); after 5th element (growth 4->8); after 8 elements (no growth)). Result: 0, 64, 64, 96, 96. Reading: first kosh (descriptor + 4x8 buffer, 16-aligned) = 64; no growth -> unchanged (64); growth to 8 (new 64-byte buffer, old 32-byte buffer leaked by bump allocator, not freed) -> 96 (live only: new buffer + descriptor, old buffer NOT counted). Delta on growth is +32 (64->96 = new 64 - old 32, live delta), NOT +64 (64->128, total delta, which would have counted the leaked old buffer). So v303 counts LIVE, correctly - the v302 'wrong parimana()' (which would have overcounted leaked buffers) is fixed for growth.
parimana.verdict: RIGHT in all three brief cases (growth live delta correct, 20k exact, block scratch freed + kosh persists), with the block-kosh 96 vs 64 as a minor diagnostic open question (32 bytes, not program results).

ws3.coverage_reflection: Probing (my method) tests RUNTIME BEHAVIOUR for cases I think of, derived from the design, the brief's bullets, and prior defects. It is good at: crashes (segfaults - R127 S1/S2/S3, all found by probing reassignment/loop cases I thought of from the tracking description); silent wrongs (stale aliases, over-reads - R127 O1-O5, all found by probing non-bare-variable sources I thought of from 'set only from a bare variable'); boundaries (capacity, growth - R129 boundary, multi-growth, interleaved, dasham, all correct); scale (20,000 koshes, 20,000,000 elements, OOM - all verified by running, which reading alone cannot prove); and regressions (re-running prior probes on new versions - R128, R129, R130 all show no regressions, which is itself valuable evidence). My R129 descriptor attack covered growth, aliasing, nesting (as far as allowed), OOM, boundaries, multiple aliases, interleaved, dasham, and scale - and found no crash/silent wrong, because FOR THE PATHS I TESTED, there was none (v302's descriptor was correct on those paths, as v303 confirms by re-running them identically). Reading (ChatGPT's method) covers EVERY CODE PATH, including edge cases I would not think to probe (off-by-one in a copy, missing check in a rarely-used path, incorrect size for a specific input). Probing covers ONLY THE PATHS I THINK OF, however thoroughly I run them (even 20M elements, if they are all on the same 'happy path' growth routine, will not hit an edge case in a different routine or a different size). ChatGPT found three by reading (SIGSEGV, silent overwrite, wrong parimana) in paths my probes did not reach, because I did not think of those specific cases. Likely candidates for what I missed (inferred, not disclosed in my brief): a specific capacity or size that triggers a particular growth path (e.g., a size where a copy loop is off by one, or where a size calculation overflows, or where a header write lands one field off); a specific buffer layout where growth overwrites an adjacent allocation (e.g., a nirmmita buffer adjacent to a kosh in a specific order, or a descriptor header adjacent to a buffer, which my nirmmita-adjacent test (one layout) did not hit, but another layout would); or a specific parimana() counting case (e.g., after a particular sequence of growth + block + growth, where the counting diverges from live, which my three parimana cases (growth, block, 20k) did not hit in that exact sequence, but another sequence would). Reading alone does NOT cover runtime/scale behaviour: that 20,000,000 numbers actually agree between two names (not just that the code looks like it should agree); that 20,000 koshes actually use one mmap (not just that the arena code looks like one mmap); that the alias cliff is actually gone at 4,194,304 and 20,000,000 (not just that descriptors 'should' fix it); that OOM is actually a message (exit 1) in practice, not a crash (reading the OOM path cannot prove the message prints and the exit is clean under a real limit - only running under ulimit proves it); or that fixes do not regress prior behaviour (only re-running prior probes proves that). Reading finds defects in code; probing proves behaviour in the world. LESSON: probing and reading are COMPLEMENTARY, not substitutes, and neither alone is sufficient. Probing finds defects in paths I think of, verifies scale/real behaviour, and catches regressions - but misses paths I do not think of (as proven by ChatGPT's three, which were in paths my R129 probes did not reach, even though my R129 probes were thorough on the paths they did cover). Reading finds defects in every code path, including edge cases I would not think of - but cannot prove runtime/scale behaviour (20M agreement, 20k one mmap, cliff gone, OOM message) or catch regressions (only re-running probes does that). FOR FUTURE WORK, the right method is BOTH, in order: READ FIRST (especially the new code - growth routine, descriptor header handling, parimana() counting - to find edge cases to probe, not just the brief's bullets), THEN PROBE WHAT YOU READ (especially edge cases: capacity 0/1/non-power-of-two, empty, single-element, large capacities, adjacent allocations in different orders, parimana() deltas (not just absolutes) after growth/block/20k sequences), PLUS KEEP THE SCALE/REGRESSION PROBES (20M/20k/cliff/OOM/re-run prior probes on every new version, because those are the only way to prove behaviour at scale and to prove fixes do not regress). My R129 probes were thorough but BULLET-BOUND (bullets + prior defects); ChatGPT's reading was CODE-BOUND (all descriptor code, not just bullets) - and code-bound found three that bullet-bound missed. Next time, I should be code-bound first, then probe.
